newsitem.title: UK: Brown shows UK Labour's radical credentials.
newsitem.headline: Brown shows UK Labour's radical credentials.

text.p: By making the Bank of England largely independent, Britain's Labour government has wasted no time in delivering on its promise to put aside dogma and push through radical reforms.
By raising interest rates just four days after taking office, Gordon Brown has established his credentials as an "Iron Chancellor" bent on taming inflation.

And by denying himself the power to set interest rates, Brown has reduced the chances of Prime Minister Tony Blair's government being blown off course by a financial crisis, as was the fate of the last two Labour administrations.

"I don't think anybody can accuse me of failing to take the tough action early on that is necessary to deal with the situation," Brown, the chancellor of the exchequer, told his maiden news conference at the Treasury on Tuesday.

Although Brown had trailed since 1993 his aim to devolve more operational responsibility for interest rates to the Bank of England, he had said the central bank would first have to build up a track record for giving sound advice.

In the event, the chancellor's aides said he had consulted carefully with senior Treasury and BoE officials for months and so had a blueprint ready to take out of his pocket within hours of Labour being swept to power last Friday.
The final decision to make the central bank all-but independent was taken by Brown, Blair, Deputy Prime Minister John Prescott and Foreign Secretary Robin Cook late on Sunday.

Explaining at length the reasons for the most sweeping changes to the Bank of England since it was founded in 1694, Brown said he wanted to put the economy on a course to deliver the low inflation needed to promote investment, growth and jobs.
"In the last century, Britain was industrially pre-eminent. The history of this century has been one of economic decline, not least because of short-termism and the pursuit of stop-go economics.
"I am determined that we make the right preparations for long-term national economic success, as we look to the century that lies ahead," Brown said.
As a keen student of history and politics, Brown was also conscious of how mistrustful financial markets had brought past governments -- both Labour and Conservative -- to their knees.
The rout of John Major's Conservatives can be traced back, analysts say, to Britain's humiliating ejection from the European Union's exchange rate mechanism in September 1992.
The former prime minister's credibility never recovered from the collapse of the centrepiece of his economic policy.

A sterling crisis torpedoed the last Labour government of James Callaghan, with then-chancellor Denis Healey being forced to turn back on the way to London's Heathrow airport to call in the International Monetary Fund for help.

Similarly, former Labour prime minister Harold Wilson was forever tainted by his belated decision to devalue the pound in 1967, after rejecting advice to do just that immediately upon winning the 1964 election.
Some analysts believe the present high level of sterling contains the seeds of a future economic crisis for Labour.
But by denying himself the power to set interest rates, Brown has ensured that the government will be at least partly shielded from the fallout of any financial market storm.
Bonds and shares soared as financial markets welcomed the decision to take party politics out of monetary policy-making.
But Brown's predecessor, Kenneth Clarke, promptly predicted that he would come to regret his decision.

"It won't be good enough for him to turn round and say It's not my responsibility guv, any more. I have handed over control to this committee You must go and complain to them if they get it wrong'. We will wait to see," Clarke told BBC radio.
